question: Is there an official 'MCP 2.0', and what is the MCP 2026-07-28 specification?
idealAnswerCore: There is no spec titled 'MCP 2.0'. The breaking release is protocol version 2026-07-28, which made the core stateless; some SDKs and blogs nicknamed that era 'v2' because it dropped the initialize handshake and session ID.
idealAnswerFraming: Interviewers often say 'MCP 2.0' loosely. Correct them politely: cite the date version, then list the headline changes. That shows you read the spec, not a tweet.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: 2026-07-28 retired initialize/initialized and Mcp-Session-Id; requests carry protocol version, client info, and capabilities in _meta
Optional server/discover replaces the old handshake for capability lookup; it is not required before tools/call
Ecosystem 'v2' names (TypeScript SDK v2, FastMCP 4, etc.) track the spec but are product versions, not the protocol name
Legacy HTTP+SSE, Roots, Sampling, and Logging are deprecated with a minimum 12-month removal window (not earlier than July 2027)

question: Why did the MCP 2026-07-28 spec make the protocol core stateless, and what still can be stateful?
idealAnswerCore: Protocol-level sessions fought load balancers, serverless, and gateways: sticky Mcp-Session-Id pinned clients to one instance. Stateless requests can hit any replica. Application state is still allowed — you mint an explicit handle from a tool and pass it back as an argument so the model can see it.
idealAnswerFraming: This is an infrastructure interview question. Contrast transport state vs business state. Hidden session maps in server memory are the anti-pattern.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Old flow: initialize → initialized + session header → every call must return to the same process or a shared session store
New flow: each JSON-RPC request is self-contained; round-robin HTTP works without Redis-for-sessions
stdio local servers still exist; the change matters most for remote Streamable HTTP at scale
If a checkout MCP needs a cart, return cartId from a tool and require it on later calls — do not hide the cart in a session cookie the model cannot name
Breaking: servers that still require initialize as the first message fail against current SDKs
idealAnswerFollowups: How would you migrate a server that stored user prefs in a Map keyed by session ID?

question: What is server/discover in MCP 2026-07-28, and how did capability negotiation move off initialize?
idealAnswerCore: Capability and identity data now ride on every request in _meta. Clients that want a catalog up front call the optional server/discover RPC; they are not required to handshake before tools/call.
idealAnswerFraming: Show you know discovery is an optimization for hosts, not a connection ritual. Mention cache hints on list results.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: _meta carries protocol version, clientInfo, and client capabilities per request
server/discover is optional; a tools/call can be the first message a replica ever sees
tools/list, prompts/list, resources/list, and resources/read responses include ttlMs and cacheScope so reconnects do not thrash catalogs or bust prompt caches
List order is deterministic to keep prefix caches stable
Hosts should still pin MCP-Protocol-Version (header and/or meta) so mixed-version fleets fail clearly
idealAnswerFollowups: When would you skip server/discover on the hot path?

question: What are Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR) in MCP, and what did they replace?
idealAnswerCore: MRTR lets a server pause a tool call by returning resultType input_required plus the questions it needs; the client retries the original method with inputResponses instead of holding an open bidirectional stream for elicitation or sampling.
idealAnswerFraming: This is how confirmations and missing fields work on a stateless transport. Compare to the old server-initiated elicitation/create over SSE.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Old model: server pushed elicitation/create, sampling/createMessage, or roots/list on a held-open stream
New model (SEP-2322): HTTP-style retry with answers attached; any replica can continue if state is in the payload/handle
Use for 'confirm destructive query' or 'need project id' without a websocket session
Sampling and Roots themselves are deprecated — do not design new features on them; MRTR is the pattern for remaining interactive needs
Hosts must bound retries so an input_required loop cannot become a cost/DoS path
idealAnswerFollowups: How would you implement a delete-table confirmation with MRTR?
Why is MRTR better for serverless than a long SSE connection?

question: Why must Streamable HTTP MCP requests include Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers?
idealAnswerCore: SEP-2243 requires Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name so gateways, WAFs, and rate limiters can route and meter without parsing JSON-RPC bodies — replacing session-id sticky routing.
idealAnswerFraming: This is a platform/gateway question. Tie it to least-privilege routing: you can allow tools/list broadly and restrict tools/call by name.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Example: Mcp-Method: tools/call and Mcp-Name: search plus MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28
Body inspection at the edge was slow, brittle, and hostile to encryption/middleware
Use headers for per-tool quotas, authz, and observability labels
Clients that omit headers fail spec-compliant servers/gateways
Does not replace argument validation — a header can lie; the host still must authz the call
idealAnswerFollowups: How would you rate-limit only expensive MCP tools at an API gateway?
What header would you log for an audit trail besides Mcp-Name?

question: How did MCP authorization change in 2026-07-28 (RFC 9207, DCR vs CIMD)?
idealAnswerCore: Auth hardened around OAuth: clients must validate the iss parameter (RFC 9207) before redeeming a code, client credentials are bound to the issuing authorization server, and Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated in favor of Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD).
idealAnswerFraming: Authorization is where teams burn integration time. Name mix-up attacks at a high level and the control (issuer check), not exploit steps.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: RFC 9207 iss on the authorization response closes authorization-server mix-up if the client actually validates it
DCR still works for a 12-month window but new designs should publish CIMD instead of registering ad hoc clients
application_type in DCR helps desktop/CLI localhost redirect URIs that used to fail OAuth checks
Enterprise Managed Authorization (EMA) is an extension for company-controlled identity, not a reason to skip per-tool consent
MCP still cannot enforce consent at the protocol layer — hosts must prompt users before powerful tools

question: What happened to MCP Tasks, and how do you run long-running work on a stateless core?
idealAnswerCore: Tasks left experimental core and became the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension: poll with tasks/get, mutate with tasks/update, cancel with tasks/cancel, and listen via subscriptions/listen instead of a dedicated GET/SSE task stream.
idealAnswerFraming: Long-running agents need durable handles, not session affinity. Mention AWS's contribution of Tasks and that extensions are opt-in.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Core protocol stays request/response; Tasks is negotiated as an extension, not assumed
Poll-based status is load-balancer friendly; old experimental subscribe loops are gone
Store task state in your DB keyed by a server-minted id the model can pass around
subscriptions/listen is an opt-in stream for notifications, not a substitute for session IDs
2025-11-25 experimental Tasks callers must migrate; error/subscription shapes changed

question: Which MCP features were deprecated in 2026-07-28, and what should new servers use instead?
idealAnswerCore: Roots, Sampling, Logging, and legacy HTTP+SSE transport are deprecated under a formal 12-month policy. New work should use explicit tool args or resource URIs instead of Roots, provider LLM APIs instead of Sampling, stderr/platform logs instead of protocol Logging, and Streamable HTTP instead of HTTP+SSE.
idealAnswerFraming: Deprecation policy is a maturity signal. Say they still work today, must not be the default in new designs, and earliest removal is about July 2027.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Roots → pass workspace/file URIs as tool arguments or resources
Sampling (server asking the client to run an LLM) → call the host's model API; avoids hidden nested-LLM sessions
Logging → stderr for stdio, and your APM for HTTP
HTTP+SSE → Streamable HTTP with method/name headers
Plan upgrades; do not wait for a hard cut that breaks production hosts

question: How do you migrate a production MCP server from the 2025-11-25 session model to 2026-07-28?
idealAnswerCore: Upgrade Tier-1 SDKs, delete initialize handlers and session maps, put per-request identity in _meta, emit Mcp-Method/Mcp-Name, and replace hidden session state with explicit handles; already-stateless wrappers are a small patch, stateful carts/workflows are the real work.
idealAnswerFraming: Walk a migration plan: inventory state, dual-run if needed, eval tools, then cut the handshake. Mention error code shifts such as missing-resource moving toward standard -32602.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Already-stateless API wrappers: drop initialize, add headers, regression-test tool schemas
Stateful servers: persist context server-side under a handle returned to the client/model
Gateways: stop routing on Mcp-Session-Id; start routing on Mcp-Method/Mcp-Name
Tasks users: move to the tasks extension poll APIs
Auth: validate iss; stop designing new DCR-only clients
Test with current SDKs that no longer send initialize — old servers fail closed

question: What is the MCP extensions framework, and what are MCP Apps versus Tasks versus EMA?
idealAnswerCore: Extensions are opt-in modules so the core can stay small: Tasks cover durable async work, MCP Apps let hosts render sandboxed UI (forms, charts) from the server, and Enterprise Managed Authorization plugs corporate identity — clients and servers must both advertise support.
idealAnswerFraming: This is the 'how does MCP grow without another breaking core' question. Contrast with stuffing features into initialize.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Core: JSON-RPC, tools, resources, prompts, stateless HTTP/stdio
Tasks: long-running operations with poll/update/cancel
MCP Apps: interactive UI in the host, sandboxed, not raw HTML execution in the model
EMA: enterprise identity/governance overlay for MCP
Skills-over-MCP (working group) is about structured agent instructions discovered via MCP, still evolving
idealAnswerFollowups: When is an MCP App better than returning Markdown from a tool?

question: How did MCP 2026-07-28 change reliability and load balancing for remote tool servers?
idealAnswerCore: Without session affinity, any healthy replica can serve tools/call; you still need idempotent tools, timeouts, and explicit handles for in-flight work — plus header-based admission control instead of sticky-session failover.
idealAnswerFraming: Connect the spec to SRE: round-robin, retries, and no Redis session cache as a SPOF. Mention MRTR retries are application-level, not TCP retries.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Health checks can hit any instance; no session store to warm
Retries after 503 must not double-execute side effects — use idempotency keys on writes
input_required retries should carry enough state to resume on another replica
Gateways shed load using Mcp-Name when one tool is hot
stdio local MCP is still a single process — do not assume the stateless benefits there
idealAnswerFollowups: How do you retry a tools/call that already started a refund?

question: Did making MCP stateless fix prompt injection or malicious-server risk?
idealAnswerCore: No. Statelessness is a scaling and routing change. Third-party servers can still exfiltrate data, confused-deputy tools can still fire, and tool results can still inject instructions — hosts still need consent, allowlists, argument authz, and untrusted-output handling.
idealAnswerFraming: Do not let infrastructure news replace threat modeling. Keep the answer defensive and high-level.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Removing sessions even reduces one class of session-fixation bugs, but that is not the main MCP threat
OAuth/CIMD/iss checks harden client registration mix-up, not tool abuse
Header routing helps enforce per-tool policy at the gateway
Tool descriptions remain untrusted unless the server is trusted
Elicitation/MRTR can social-engineer users — confirm UX must show what will execute

question: How should a production host (IDE, desktop agent, or SaaS copilot) pin and roll out MCP protocol versions?
idealAnswerCore: Pin MCP-Protocol-Version, dual-run 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28 only with an adapter, catalog servers that still need initialize, and treat a spec bump like a dependency upgrade: eval tools, auth, and headers before flipping the default SDK.
idealAnswerFraming: Platform ownership. New SDKs stop sending initialize, so an unplanned upgrade is an outage for lagging servers.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: Inventory: local stdio vs remote HTTP, protocol version, whether the server is stateful
Feature-flag the new client; canary internal servers first
Reject mixed headers (session id without method name) in your gateway logs
Keep a compatibility layer only as a time-boxed exception
Document user impact: some community servers will break until they upgrade

question: How do MCP Host, Client, and Server differ, and who talks to the LLM?
idealAnswerCore: The Host is the application (Cursor, Claude Desktop, your agent service). The Client is the MCP connector inside that host. The Server exposes tools/resources/prompts. The LLM only sees tool schemas and results that the host puts in the model API — it does not speak MCP on the wire.
idealAnswerFraming: This misconception shows up constantly. Draw the three boxes. Function calling sits between host and model; MCP sits between host client and server.
idealAnswerKeyPoints: One host can run many clients, each connected to a different server
stdio servers are child processes of the host; HTTP servers are remote
The model never receives Mcp-Method headers; the host translates tool_calls ↔ tools/call
Security consent belongs in the host UI, not in the model weights
Getting this wrong leads people to 'prompt the MCP server' as if it were the model
